intro.uz: Fikr-mulohaza (opinion) matni: tarjimonlik sanʼati, aniqlik va ravonlik, «tarjima qilib boʻlmaydigan» soʻzlar, sheʼr va hazil tarjimasi. Bu matnda T/F/NG savollari YES / NO / NOT GIVEN maʼnosida: T = muallif shunday fikrda, F = muallif buning aksini aytadi, NG = muallifning fikri berilmagan. Taxminan 20 daqiqa: muallif oʻz fikrini bildiradigan joylarni («In my view», «I find», «I suspect») belgilab oling — YES/NO savollarining kaliti shu yerda.

paragraphs.en: Translators are fond of describing their work as building bridges between cultures, and the metaphor is an attractive one. It suggests a solid structure across which meaning passes intact from one bank to the other. Yet anyone who has attempted to translate a demanding text knows that the reality is rather less tidy. Meaning does not simply cross over; it has to be reconstructed, and at every stage the translator must make choices that no dictionary can make for them. An old Italian pun equates the translator with a traitor, and while the charge is unfair, it captures an uncomfortable truth: every translation involves some loss, and the question is never whether to sacrifice something but what.

The oldest debate in the field concerns the competing demands of fidelity and fluency. Since antiquity, commentators have argued over whether a translator should follow the original word for word or render its sense in whatever form sounds most natural in the target language. A strictly literal version may preserve the structure of the source but often reads awkwardly, while a highly fluent one may read beautifully yet quietly erase everything that made the original distinctive. In my view, neither extreme deserves to be treated as a virtue. A good translation should read as though it had been written with care in its new language, while still allowing the reader to sense that it came from somewhere else.

Much is made of so-called untranslatable words, and lists of them circulate widely as evidence that some ideas exist in one language alone. Consider the Uzbek word hashar, which refers to the custom of neighbours gathering voluntarily to help with a shared task such as building a house or cleaning a street. English can offer community work or voluntary labour, but neither phrase conveys the sense of reciprocity and celebration that usually accompanies the practice. Nevertheless, it would be misleading to conclude that such words cannot be translated at all. Their meaning can almost always be explained; what is lost is the economy with which a single word carries an entire cluster of associations.

Poetry presents these difficulties in their most acute form, because in verse the sound of a line is inseparable from its sense. Classical Uzbek poetry, much of it composed in the quantitative metre known as aruz, relies on patterns of long and short syllables that English, with its stress-based rhythms, cannot reproduce. A translator must therefore decide whether to imitate the rhyme scheme at the cost of accuracy, abandon form in favour of meaning, or seek some compromise between the two. Each option produces a different poem, and readers who know only one version should remember that they are encountering an interpretation rather than the original itself.

Humour is perhaps even more treacherous. Jokes that depend on wordplay rarely survive the journey intact, since a pun is by definition tied to the accidents of a particular language. Humour that arises from situations, by contrast, often travels surprisingly well. The anecdotes about Afandi, the folk trickster familiar across much of the Turkic and Persian-speaking world, tend to work in English precisely because their comedy lies in the logic of the situation rather than in the words. Where a joke relies on shared cultural knowledge, however, the translator faces an unenviable choice between adding an explanation, which kills the joke, and substituting a local equivalent, which changes it.

Despite the decisive role they play, translators have traditionally been expected to remain unseen. Their names are frequently omitted from book covers, and reviewers often praise a novel's style without acknowledging that the sentences they admire were written by someone other than the author. One scholar has memorably described this situation as the translator's invisibility, arguing that the ideal of a perfectly smooth translation conceals the labour behind it. I find this argument persuasive. Readers would arguably be better served if translators were credited prominently and allowed to explain, in a preface or afterword, the principles that guided their decisions.

None of this is cause for despair. Translation is imperfect in the same way that all reading is imperfect: every reader brings their own experience to a text and takes away something slightly different. Far from being a regrettable necessity, translation is one of the main ways in which literatures renew themselves, since encounters with foreign works have repeatedly introduced new forms and ideas into national traditions. Machine translation may increasingly handle routine documents, but rendering a novel or a poem will, I suspect, continue to require human judgement for some time to come.

title.uz: Ellipsis: takrorni tushirib qoldirish (… but what)

grammar.example: the question is never whether to sacrifice something but what

questions.statement: The writer believes the image of a bridge accurately reflects what translators do.

explain.uz: NO: «the reality is rather less tidy. Meaning does not simply cross over; it has to be reconstructed» — muallif metaforani yetarli deb hisoblamaydi.

questions.statement: The writer accepts that some loss is unavoidable in any translation.

explain.uz: YES: «every translation involves some loss» — muallif buni «uncomfortable truth» deb tan oladi.

questions.statement: According to the writer, a good translation should hide every trace of its foreign origin.

explain.uz: NO: «while still allowing the reader to sense that it came from somewhere else» — begonalikni butunlay yashirmaslik kerak.

questions.statement: The writer thinks that most lists of untranslatable words are compiled by professional translators.

explain.uz: NOT GIVEN: roʻyxatlar keng tarqalgani aytilgan, lekin ularni kim tuzishi haqida muallif fikri yoʻq.

questions.statement: The writer considers humour based on situations easier to translate than humour based on wordplay.

explain.uz: YES: wordplay «rarely survive the journey intact», situational humour esa «often travels surprisingly well».

questions.statement: The writer argues that translators of literature should be paid more than they currently are.

explain.uz: NOT GIVEN: muallif tarjimonlar nomi koʻrsatilishi va soʻzboshi yozishini taklif qiladi, ammo haq toʻlash haqida gapirmaydi.

questions.statement: The writer is confident that machines will soon translate novels as well as humans do.

explain.uz: NO: «rendering a novel or a poem will, I suspect, continue to require human judgement for some time to come».

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main point about the word hashar?
options: It has no meaning that an English speaker could understand.
Its meaning can be explained, but not as concisely as in Uzbek.
It proves that Uzbek is richer in vocabulary than English.
Translators should always leave it in its original form.

explain.uz: «Their meaning can almost always be explained; what is lost is the economy with which a single word carries an entire cluster of associations» — «economy» = qisqalik, ixchamlik.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the metre known as aruz?
options: to show that classical Uzbek poetry has no rhyme
to give an example of a formal feature that English cannot reproduce
to argue that poetry should be translated as prose
to explain why Uzbek readers prefer classical poetry

explain.uz: «relies on patterns of long and short syllables that English, with its stress-based rhythms, cannot reproduce» — sheʼriy shakl tarjimada saqlanmasligiga misol.

questions.prompt: In paragraph E, what does the phrase "which kills the joke" refer to?

explain.uz: «adding an explanation, which kills the joke» — «which» oʻzidan oldingi iboraga ishora qiladi. Mahalliy muqobil esa hazilni «changes», yaʼni oʻzgartiradi.

questions.prompt: What does the writer recommend in paragraph F?
options: Reviewers should stop commenting on the style of translated novels.
Translations should be as smooth as possible so that readers forget the translator.
Translators should be given visible credit and a chance to explain their approach.
Publishers should print the original text alongside the translation.

explain.uz: «translators were credited prominently and allowed to explain, in a preface or afterword, the principles that guided their decisions».

questions.prompt: A strictly literal translation may keep the structure of the source but often reads ___.

explain.uz: «A strictly literal version may preserve the structure of the source but often reads awkwardly».

questions.prompt: English phrases such as community work fail to convey the sense of ___ and celebration that hashar involves.

explain.uz: «neither phrase conveys the sense of reciprocity and celebration».

questions.prompt: One scholar has called the hidden position of translators the translator's ___.

explain.uz: «One scholar has memorably described this situation as the translator's invisibility».
